# Exercise 9.2 — SHAP values: global and local explanations {#sec-shap}

Exercise 9.1 ranked the variables for the forest as a whole. It did not say
which way a variable pushes the risk, and it said nothing about any one
patient. **SHAP values** do both. For every patient and every variable, a SHAP
value says how much that variable moved this patient's predicted probability
away from the average prediction.

**Goal.** In this exercise you will:

- compute SHAP values for the test patients and check that they add up to the
  prediction;
- read two global plots: the mean absolute SHAP bar plot and the beeswarm;
- read the waterfall plot for one patient.

::: {.callout-note}
## The plots are for looking at
The code for every plot is folded away just above it, in case you are curious,
and all of it is in the notebook linked at the top of each tab. You are not
expected to write it yourself.
:::

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "ranger", "kernelshap", "shapviz"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(kernelshap)            # computes SHAP values for any model
library(shapviz)               # plots SHAP values

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables
```

The same data ([`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv)), outcome
and five predictors as Exercise 9.1.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))
```

As always, 80% of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as
the test set.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)
```

The same random forest as Exercise 9.1, fitted on the training rows and
evaluated once on the test rows.

```{r}
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(1)
rf_fit <- rf_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(rf_fit, new_data = test))

roc_auc(test_preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

The forest reaches a test AUC of 0.753.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — SHAP values for the test patients

Start from the **baseline**: the average prediction. A patient's SHAP values
share out the gap between the baseline and that patient's prediction, one
piece per variable. A positive value pushes the risk **up**; a negative value
pushes it **down**. Added together, they give the prediction exactly:

**baseline + the SHAP values of all variables = the prediction.**

**kernelshap** computes SHAP values for any model. A variable we "do not know"
is filled in from a **background** sample of 100 training patients. We explain
the 150 test patients, and **shapviz** keeps the values for the probability of
`pos`. This takes about 15 seconds.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
background <- train |>
  slice_sample(n = 100) |>
  select(-diabetes)

shap_rf <- kernelshap(rf_fit, X = test |> select(-diabetes), bg_X = background,
                      type = "prob", verbose = FALSE)

sv_pos <- shapviz(shap_rf)$.pred_pos       # SHAP values for the probability of pos

dim(get_shap_values(sv_pos))               # one row per patient, one column per predictor
get_baseline(sv_pos)                       # the average prediction
```

The baseline is 0.364. Now check that it adds up for the first test patient.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
patient_shap <- get_shap_values(sv_pos)[1, ]
patient_shap

get_baseline(sv_pos) + ______(patient_shap)
test_preds$.pred_pos[1]
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
You want to add up the five SHAP values in `patient_shap`. The R function that
adds up a vector is `sum()`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
patient_shap <- get_shap_values(sv_pos)[1, ]
patient_shap

get_baseline(sv_pos) + sum(patient_shap)
test_preds$.pred_pos[1]
```

Both lines give 0.706. Glucose contributes by far the most (+0.353).
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — The global view: bar plot and beeswarm

We now have 150 × 5 SHAP values. The **mean absolute SHAP value** of a
variable says how far, on average, it moves a patient's prediction, up or
down. It is a variable importance, in units of probability.

```{r}
get_shap_values(sv_pos) |>
  abs() |>
  colMeans() |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE)
```

Glucose moves a prediction by 0.162 on average. The other four variables move
it by between 0.027 and 0.066.

The bar plot draws the same numbers:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
sv_importance(sv_pos, fill = "steelblue")
```

The **beeswarm** shows every patient. Each dot is one patient's SHAP value for
one variable. The colour is the patient's value of that variable, from low to
high.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
sv_importance(sv_pos, kind = "beeswarm")
```

**Question!** In the glucose row, where are the patients with high glucose,
and where are those with low glucose?

High glucose sits on the right: it pushes the risk up, by as much as 0.424.
Low glucose sits on the left and pushes it down, by as much as 0.362. The bar
plot gives only the size of each effect. The beeswarm also gives its direction,
patient by patient.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — One patient: the waterfall plot

A **local** explanation answers: *why did the model give this patient this
risk?* Take the first test patient again:

```{r}
test_preds |>
  slice(1) |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes, .pred_pos)
```

She is 28, with no pregnancies, a BMI of 28.5 and a glucose of 194 mg/dL, and
she does **not** have diabetes. The waterfall plot starts at the baseline at
the bottom and adds one SHAP value at a time, up to her prediction at the top.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
sv_waterfall(sv_pos, row_id = 1)
```

Read in words: the average patient has a predicted risk of 0.364. Her very high
glucose adds 0.353. Her other values change it by 0.035 or less. Her predicted
risk is 0.706, so at a threshold of 0.5 she is a false positive. The
explanation tells us what the model did, not whether it was right.

**Your turn.** Draw the waterfall for the test patient the model thinks is at
**highest** risk.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
highest <- which.max(test_preds$______)     # the row number of the highest probability
test_preds |> slice(highest)

sv_waterfall(sv_pos, row_id = ______)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`which.max()` returns the position of the largest value in a vector. The vector
you want is the predicted probability of `pos`. Then pass that position as
`row_id`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
highest <- which.max(test_preds$.pred_pos)
test_preds |> slice(highest)

sv_waterfall(sv_pos, row_id = highest)
```

She is 27, with no pregnancies, a glucose of 181 and a BMI of 49.6, and a
predicted risk of 0.922. She does have diabetes. Every variable pushes her risk
up: glucose by 0.358, BMI by 0.105, and the other three by 0.042 or less.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points
- A SHAP value is one variable's push on one patient's prediction, up or down from the baseline (the average prediction).
- Baseline + the SHAP values of all variables = the prediction, exactly.
- Mean absolute SHAP ranks the variables; the beeswarm also shows the direction of each effect.
- The waterfall plot explains one patient's prediction. It says what the model did, not whether the model was right.
:::

### Packages and data

```{python}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn shap

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import shap

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
```

The same data ([`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv)), outcome
and five predictors as Exercise 9.1.

```{python}
diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "diabetes"]]
diabetes["diabetes"] = (diabetes["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)       # 1 = pos, 0 = neg

predictors = ["pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age"]
```

As always, 80% of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as
the test set.

```{python}
train, test = train_test_split(diabetes, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
```

The same random forest as Exercise 9.1, fitted on the training rows and
evaluated once on the test rows.

```{python}
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
rf = rf.fit(train[predictors], train["diabetes"])

test_prob = rf.predict_proba(test[predictors])[:, 1]    # probability of diabetes

print("test AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(test["diabetes"], test_prob), 3))
```

The forest reaches a test AUC of 0.794.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — SHAP values for the test patients

Start from the **baseline**: the average prediction. A patient's SHAP values
share out the gap between the baseline and that patient's prediction, one
piece per variable. A positive value pushes the risk **up**; a negative value
pushes it **down**. Added together, they give the prediction exactly:

**baseline + the SHAP values of all variables = the prediction.**

The **shap** package's `TreeExplainer` uses the structure of the trees to
compute exact SHAP values in under a second. We explain the 150 test patients
and keep the values for class 1, diabetes.

```{python}
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(rf)
explanation = explainer(test[predictors])

shap_pos = explanation[:, :, 1]            # SHAP values for class 1 (diabetes)

print("shape:   ", shap_pos.values.shape)  # one row per patient, one column per predictor
print("baseline:", round(shap_pos.base_values[0], 3))   # the average prediction
```

The baseline is 0.359. Now check that it adds up for the first test patient.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
patient_shap = shap_pos.values[0]
print(np.round(patient_shap, 3))

print(shap_pos.base_values[0] + patient_shap.______())
print(test_prob[0])
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
You want to add up the five SHAP values in `patient_shap`. NumPy arrays have a
`.sum()` method.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
patient_shap = shap_pos.values[0]
print(np.round(patient_shap, 3))

print(shap_pos.base_values[0] + patient_shap.sum())
print(test_prob[0])
```

Both lines give 0.276. Glucose contributes the most, and pushes this patient's
risk down (−0.139).
:::
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — The global view: bar plot and beeswarm

We now have 150 × 5 SHAP values. The **mean absolute SHAP value** of a
variable says how far, on average, it moves a patient's prediction, up or
down. It is a variable importance, in units of probability.

```{python}
shap_importance = pd.Series(np.abs(shap_pos.values).mean(axis=0), index=predictors)

shap_importance.sort_values(ascending=False).round(3)
```

Glucose moves a prediction by 0.159 on average. The other four variables move
it by between 0.034 and 0.066.

The bar plot draws the same numbers:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
shap.plots.bar(shap_pos, show=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The **beeswarm** shows every patient. Each dot is one patient's SHAP value for
one variable. The colour is the patient's value of that variable, blue low and
red high.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
shap.plots.beeswarm(shap_pos, show=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Question!** In the glucose row, where are the patients with high glucose,
and where are those with low glucose?

High glucose sits on the right: it pushes the risk up, by as much as 0.480.
Low glucose sits on the left and pushes it down, by as much as 0.313. The bar
plot gives only the size of each effect. The beeswarm also gives its direction,
patient by patient.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — One patient: the waterfall plot

A **local** explanation answers: *why did the model give this patient this
risk?* Take the first test patient again:

```{python}
patient = test.iloc[[0]]                   # double brackets keep it a one-row table
print(patient)
print("predicted probability:", round(test_prob[0], 3))
```

She is 35, with 6 pregnancies, a BMI of 28.8 and a glucose of 115 mg/dL, and
she does **not** have diabetes. The waterfall plot starts at the baseline at
the bottom and adds one SHAP value at a time, up to her prediction at the top.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| fig-height: 3.5
shap.plots.waterfall(shap_pos[0], show=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read in words: the average patient has a predicted risk of 0.359. Her ordinary
glucose takes 0.139 off. Her age, BMI and pregnancies each add a little (0.032
or less), and her pedigree function takes off 0.021. Her predicted risk is
0.276: below 0.5, so she is correctly predicted as `neg`.

**Your turn.** Draw the waterfall for the test patient the model thinks is at
**highest** risk.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
highest = test_prob.______()                # the position of the highest probability
print(test.iloc[[highest]])

shap.plots.waterfall(shap_pos[______], show=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
NumPy arrays have `.argmax()`, the position of the largest value. Then use that
position to pick the patient out of `shap_pos`.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
highest = test_prob.argmax()
print(test.iloc[[highest]])

shap.plots.waterfall(shap_pos[highest], show=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

She is 27, with no pregnancies, a glucose of 165 and a BMI of 42.1, and a
predicted risk of 0.992. Every variable pushes her risk up: glucose by 0.425,
BMI by 0.074, and the other three by 0.063 or less. She does **not** have
diabetes. The model's most confident prediction in the test set is wrong, and
nothing in the explanation would tell you so.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points
- A SHAP value is one variable's push on one patient's prediction, up or down from the baseline (the average prediction).
- Baseline + the SHAP values of all variables = the prediction, exactly.
- Mean absolute SHAP ranks the variables; the beeswarm also shows the direction of each effect.
- The waterfall plot explains one patient's prediction. It says what the model did, not whether the model was right.
:::

::::::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Teaching choice.** Three key messages only: SHAP values add up to the
prediction; the bar plot and beeswarm give the global view; the waterfall reads
one patient. The old Part 4 (logistic regression and all importance measures
side by side) and the stretch tasks were removed. The split is now the usual
80/20 random split, so R and Python have different test patients and quote
their own numbers. The model is unchanged (500 trees, ranger / scikit-learn,
forest seed 1). The SHAP idea can be one board diagram: baseline, arrows up
and down, prediction.

**Expected values.** R (`set.seed(42)` split, forest `set.seed(1)`,
background `set.seed(1)`, 100 rows): 600 training and 150 test people; test
AUC 0.753; baseline 0.364. First test patient (pregnant 0, glucose 194, mass
28.5, pedigree 0.24, age 28, neg): predicted 0.706; SHAP glucose +0.353, age
+0.035, pedigree −0.032, pregnant −0.012, mass −0.001. Mean |SHAP|: glucose
0.162, mass 0.066, age 0.055, pregnant 0.047, pedigree 0.027. Glucose SHAP
from −0.362 to +0.424. Highest-risk patient (pregnant 0, glucose 181, mass
49.6, pedigree 0.687, age 27, pos): predicted 0.922; glucose +0.358, mass
+0.105, pedigree +0.042, pregnant +0.036, age +0.017.
Python (`random_state=42` split, forest `random_state=1`): test AUC 0.794;
baseline 0.359 (TreeExplainer, close to the training prevalence 0.360). First
test patient (pregnant 6, glucose 115, mass 28.8, pedigree 0.368, age 35,
neg): predicted 0.276; SHAP glucose −0.139, age +0.032, mass +0.026, pedigree
−0.021, pregnant +0.017. Mean |SHAP|: glucose 0.159, age 0.066, mass 0.060,
pregnant 0.049, pedigree 0.034. Glucose SHAP from −0.313 to +0.480.
Highest-risk patient (pregnant 0, glucose 165, mass 42.1, pedigree 0.399, age
27, neg): predicted 0.992, a confident false positive; glucose +0.425, mass
+0.074, pregnant +0.063, age +0.039, pedigree +0.031.

**Common failures.** (1) Taking the SHAP values of class 0 (Python
`explanation[:, :, 0]`, R `.pred_neg`): every sign flips. (2) Expecting R and
Python to agree: the splits, the forests and the way "unknown" variables are
filled in (background sample versus tree paths) all differ. (3) In R, leaving
out `type = "prob"` in `kernelshap()`: it then stops with an error.

**Timing.** kernelshap takes about 15 seconds; TreeExplainer under one second.
Part 1 fifteen minutes, Part 2 fifteen, Part 3 fifteen.
:::
:::
